title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array — binary search on inflection.
shortTitle: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array — Binary Search on Inflection

s1_definition.profdef: A rotated sorted array is a sorted array that has been shifted so it wraps around at one pivot point, and finding its minimum means locating that pivot, the single place where a larger element is immediately followed by a smaller one. Binary search locates it in logarithmic time by comparing the middle element to the right boundary: if the middle is greater than the right, the minimum lies to the right of middle, otherwise it is at middle or to its left. It runs in logarithmic time with constant space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a list of interest-rate checkpoints that were sorted ascending but then rotated because the cycle restarted partway through the year, and an analyst needs the lowest rate, which sits exactly at the point where the sequence drops from a high back to its restart low. Instead of scanning all checkpoints, the analyst repeatedly looks at the middle checkpoint and compares it to the last one, throwing away half the list each time, to home in on that single drop point.
s1_definition.oneliner: Compare middle to the right boundary and keep the half that still contains the drop point.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A rotated sorted array is a sorted array that has been shifted so it wraps around at one pivot point, and finding its minimum means locating that pivot, the single place where a larger element is immediately followed by a smaller one. Binary search locates it in logarithmic time by comparing the middle element to the right boundary: if the middle is greater than the right, the minimum lies to the right of middle, otherwise it is at middle or to its left. It runs in logarithmic time with constant space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a list of interest-rate checkpoints that were sorted ascending but then rotated because the cycle restarted partway through the year, and an analyst needs the lowest rate, which sits exactly at the point where the sequence drops from a high back to its restart low. Instead of scanning all checkpoints, the analyst repeatedly looks at the middle checkpoint and compares it to the last one, throwing away half the list each time, to home in on that single drop point.

**One line to remember:** Compare middle to the right boundary and keep the half that still contains the drop point.

sections.s2_technical:
A sorted array rotated at some pivot has two sorted runs: a higher run at the front and a lower run at the back, with the overall minimum sitting at the very start of the back run, which is the pivot. The naive approach scans for the one place where an element is greater than its next neighbor, which is linear. Binary search finds the pivot in logarithmic time by always keeping the half that must contain it.

You keep a left and right index over the whole array. At each step you compute the middle index and compare the element at middle to the element at right, the current right boundary. If the middle element is greater than the right element, then the pivot, and therefore the minimum, must be somewhere strictly to the right of middle, because a sorted run would never have its middle larger than its end, so you set left to middle plus one. Otherwise the middle element is less than or equal to the right element, meaning the run from middle to right is properly sorted and the minimum is at middle or to its left, so you set right to middle. You stop when left equals right, and that index holds the minimum.

Comparing to the right boundary rather than the left is deliberate and important. If you compared middle to left instead, a fully non-rotated array, or certain rotations, would be ambiguous and you would need extra cases. Comparing to right cleanly decides which half holds the pivot in every rotation, including zero rotation where the array is already sorted and the answer is the first element.

A senior point is the handling of duplicates. If the array can contain duplicate values, the comparison of middle to right can tie, and when the middle equals the right you cannot tell which half holds the minimum, so you safely shrink the right boundary by one. That degrades the worst case to linear when the array is all equal values, which is unavoidable, but keeps it logarithmic on average. For distinct values this extra case is not needed.

Another senior point is money precision. If the checkpoints are amounts I compare with BigDecimal compareTo rather than primitive operators, so exact decimal values are ordered correctly. I guard the empty array by rejecting it and a single-element array returns that element immediately.

A small finance-domain example: `int lo=0,hi=n-1; while(lo<hi){ int mid=(lo+hi)>>>1; if(rates[mid].compareTo(rates[hi])>0) lo=mid+1; else hi=mid; } return rates[lo];` returns the lowest rate in logarithmic time.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps interest-rate checkpoints that were recorded in ascending order but then rotated because the rate cycle restarted mid-year, and a treasury feature must quickly find the lowest rate in that rotated list, which marks the cycle restart. The list can be long and the feature is called frequently. Finding the minimum in a rotated sorted array with binary search is exactly this.

This is exactly how Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array works in Java — binary search comparing the middle to the right boundary to keep the half containing the drop point.

Problem 2 — Some years the cycle did not rotate at all, so the list is already sorted and the answer is the first element, and rates are exact BigDecimal values. This shows the zero-rotation edge case and money precision.

What the code will do: a `RotatedArraySearch` with `findMinimumRate(BigDecimal[] rates)` using binary search on the inflection, comparing to the right boundary. The demo finds the lowest rate in a rotated checkpoint list.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the rotated rate checkpoints are `4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2`.

Step 1: lo is zero and hi is six. The middle index is three, holding `7`. We compare `7` to the right boundary `2`. Since `7` is greater than `2`, the drop point and the minimum must be strictly to the right, so lo becomes four.

Step 2: lo is four and hi is six. The middle index is five, holding `1`. We compare `1` to the right boundary `2`. Since `1` is not greater than `2`, the run from middle to right is sorted and the minimum is at middle or to its left, so hi becomes five.

Step 3: lo is four and hi is five. The middle index is four, holding `0`. We compare `0` to the right boundary at index five, which is `1`. Since `0` is not greater than `1`, hi becomes four.

Step 4: now lo equals hi at index four, so the loop ends. The element at index four is `0`, which is the minimum. The search touched only three middles instead of scanning all seven elements, which is the logarithmic saving.

Step 5: for the already-sorted demo `1, 2, 3, 4`, every middle is less than or equal to the right boundary, so hi keeps shrinking toward the left and the answer is the first element `1`, confirming the zero-rotation case works with the same code.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T18:50:00Z INFO Minimum rate at index 4 = 0
2026-10-26T18:50:00Z INFO Lowest rate (rotated) = 0
2026-10-26T18:50:00Z INFO Minimum rate at index 0 = 1
2026-10-26T18:50:00Z INFO Lowest rate (no rotation) = 1
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]  lo=0 hi=6
    │
    ▼
  while lo<hi: mid=(lo+hi)/2; cmp a[mid] vs a[hi]
    │ mid3=7 > a[hi]=2 → lo=4  (pivot to the right)
    │ mid5=1 <= a[hi]=2 → hi=5
    │ mid4=0 <= a[5]=1 → hi=4
    │ lo==hi==4
    ▼
  minimum = a[4] = 0
    ▼
  Output: lowest rate (cycle restart point)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Rotated Minimum Search ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Binary search on inflection: compare mid to RIGHT boundary   │
  │  Invariant: the kept half always contains the pivot (min)     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: search class only finds the rotated minimum               │
  │  O: add a duplicate-aware branch without changing callers     │
  │  D: callers depend on BigDecimal result, not the index math   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          RotatedArraySearch           │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + findMinimumRate(rates)              │  BigDecimal, O(log n)
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      findMinimumRate contract:
        Pre:  rates non-empty, distinct, rotated-sorted
        Post: returns the smallest element (the pivot)
        Compare mid to hi; never to lo (avoids ambiguity)

  ── State Diagram: Search Window ──────────────────────────

  [lo<hi] ──a[mid]>a[hi]? lo=mid+1 : hi=mid──→ [narrow window]
      │ lo==hi
      ▼
  [DONE: a[lo]]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. RotatedMinDemo.main()
  2.   → findMinimumRate([4,5,6,7,0,1,2])
  3.     → compare mid to hi, discard half
  4.     → converge to pivot index 4
  5.     → return 0
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array locates the pivot of a sorted array that has been rotated, the single point where a larger element is immediately followed by a smaller one, which is where the minimum sits. I solve it with binary search in logarithmic time and constant space by comparing the middle element to the right boundary: if the middle is greater than the right, the pivot must be strictly to the right of middle, otherwise it is at middle or to its left.

Comparing to the right boundary rather than the left is the deliberate choice that makes this clean. Comparing to the left leaves fully sorted or certain rotations ambiguous and forces extra cases, whereas comparing to the right cleanly decides which half holds the pivot in every rotation, including the zero-rotation case where the array is already sorted and the answer is simply the first element.

The senior nuance is duplicates. When values can repeat, the middle can tie with the right boundary and you cannot tell which half holds the minimum, so you safely shrink the right boundary by one, which degrades the worst case to linear for an all-equal array but keeps it logarithmic otherwise. For distinct values that extra branch is unnecessary, and I compare with BigDecimal compareTo so exact decimal rates are ordered correctly.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on interest-rate checkpoints that were recorded ascending but rotated when the rate cycle restarted mid-year, letting the treasury feature find the lowest rate, the cycle restart, instantly even over a long list. Explaining the compare-to-the-right-boundary reasoning, the zero-rotation case, and the duplicate handling shows the interviewer that I understand why this binary search is structured the way it is.
